value.body: A clinical pharmacist works on hospital wards with doctors and nurses to make sure patients get the right medicines at the right doses. Hospitals, especially larger private and teaching hospitals, hire them. A typical day involves reviewing prescriptions, checking for drug interactions, counselling patients, and reporting side effects.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: Pharm.D (6 years including internship), or Pharm.D (Post Baccalaureate) after B.Pharm

items.label: Regulator
items.value: Pharmacy Council of India; registration with a State Pharmacy Council

items.label: Where the work is
items.value: Hospital wards, ICUs, drug information centres

items.label: Pharm.D enrolment
items.source: AISHE 2023-24, Ministry of Education (programme-wise enrolment, all modes)

items.label: Registered pharmacists in India
items.note: All registered pharmacists, not only clinical pharmacists

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Complete a Pharm.D (entry after Class 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Biology or Maths), including the hospital internship year, and register with your State Pharmacy Council. Freshers usually apply to hospitals with clinical pharmacy departments; internships at those hospitals often help.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Spotting drug interactions and dosing errors

value.title: At a glance
items: Dedicated clinical pharmacist posts are still limited in many Indian hospitals.
Many Pharm.D graduates also move into pharmacovigilance, clinical research or roles abroad.
Growth can lead to senior clinical pharmacist, drug information or teaching roles.
